0.title: A Farewell Letter from the Rock
0.overview:
Second Peter is the apostle's last will and testament. Writing in the shadow of his own death — 'the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me' (1:14; cf. John 21:18–19) — Peter addresses a church under pressure from false teachers who have crept inside the community, twisted Paul's letters, and weaponized a crude uniformitarianism against the hope of Christ's return. The letter's three movements answer three threats: the erosion of moral seriousness (ch. 1: grow in the divine nature), the corruption of doctrine by immoral teachers (ch. 2: their condemnation is certain), and the mocking of eschatological hope (ch. 3: the Day is coming and it will be unlike anything the world has seen).

The letter's authorship is the most contested in the NT canon. The vocabulary differs sharply from 1 Peter, and Origen already noted that some doubted it. Eusebius placed it among the antilegomena — letters known but disputed. Yet the arguments for Petrine authorship are substantial: the self-identification is unusually specific (Simeon Peter, v.1; the eyewitness claim of vv.16–18; the reference to a prior letter in 3:1); a forger who fabricates this much personal detail is extraordinarily bold. The vocabulary difference most likely reflects a different secretary — 1 Peter was written dia Silouanou (through Silvanus, 1 Pet 5:12), while 2 Peter's quite different style may reflect Peter writing without that help, or with another. The church ultimately recognized it as canonical, and its theological weight — the virtue chain, the transfiguration testimony, the patience of God, the new creation — fully justifies that recognition.

The relationship to Jude is unavoidable: 2 Peter 2 and Jude share extensive material (the angels who sinned, Sodom and Gomorrah, the Balaam archetype, waterless clouds, the scoffers of the last days). The majority of scholars believe Peter used Jude (not the reverse), which, if correct, places 2 Peter after Jude and in the mid-to-late 60s AD — consistent with Peter's death under Nero (c. 64–68 AD). Peter does not merely copy Jude; he develops, expands, and re-focuses the material for a church whose crisis has moved from external pressure to internal corruption.

1.title: Partakers of the Divine Nature
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ:<sup>2</sup>May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.<sup>3</sup>His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence,<sup>4</sup>by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.<sup>5</sup>For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and 1.overview:
Chapter 1 lays the foundation. God’s power has already given believers everything they need for life and godliness (v. 3). On that gift rests the command: make every effort to add to your faith, and so confirm your calling (vv. 5, 10). Gift first, then effort: that is the grammar of grace.

The second half grounds Peter’s message in two witnesses that agree: the apostles saw Christ’s glory at the transfiguration, and the prophetic Scriptures, spoken by men carried along by the Holy Spirit, point to the same Christ and his coming day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Divine Power and Precious Promises
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to believers whose faith is of equal value to his own. God’s power has given them everything for life and godliness, and his promises make them sharers in his holy nature. So they must make every effort to grow in a chain of qualities from faith to love. Those who grow are kept from fruitlessness and confirm that God has called them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Partakers of the Divine Nature

God's power has already granted everything needed for life and godliness. Sharing the divine nature means sharing his holiness, not becoming God — and growth in the qualities of verses 5–7 is how a believer confirms his calling.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter told readers who had seen nothing that their faith was of equal standing with his.

Now: When growth stalls, look first for a memory of forgiveness that has grown dim (v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter, Christ’s servant and apostle, writes to those who have received a faith just as precious as the apostles’, through the righteousness of Jesus Christ, our God and Saviour, and prays for grace and peace to grow as they know God and Jesus better.

Simeon Peter. He uses the Hebrew form of his name and the name Jesus gave him: the fisherman and the rock. And “servant” comes before “apostle”.

Equal standing. Faith is “obtained”, a word for receiving by lot: a gift, not an achievement. And it is of equal value to that of an eyewitness. There is no second-class faith for those who came later.

“Our God and Savior Jesus Christ”. One Greek article governs both titles, marking them as one person, as in Titus 2:13. Peter calls Jesus God.

Knowledge. The word (epignōsis) is the letter’s key word, the true knowledge of God and Christ, against false teachers offering a different kind.
verseByVerse.note: Peter’s farewell letter, written as he expected to die soon (1:14), probably from Rome in the mid 60s AD. “Simeon” is the Hebrew form of his name.

verseByVerse.quote: His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence, by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s divine power has already given us everything we need for life and godliness, through knowing Christ, who called us to his glory. Through his great promises we come to share in God’s nature, having escaped the corruption caused by evil desires.

Already given. The tense is complete. No extra secret is needed. Anyone offering a further instalment of spiritual knowledge is selling something that does not exist.

What “partakers of the divine nature” does not mean. It does not mean we become God or are absorbed into him. The Creator and the creature remain distinct. It means sharing his moral character and life: holiness, incorruption, the opposite of the world’s corruption that the verse goes on to mention. Some Eastern Orthodox teaching speaks of “deification” here; Reformed readers prefer to speak of union with Christ and renewal in God’s image, which is what Peter describes.

On a Tuesday. A Christian feels he lacks what others have: more gifts, a deeper experience. Peter says you already have everything you need for godliness in Christ. The question is not what you are missing, but whether you are using what you have.

verseByVerse.quote: For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness, and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God has given so much, make every effort to add to your faith a growing chain of qualities: virtue, knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, godliness, brotherly affection and love.

Gift, then effort. “For this very reason” points back to what God has given. The effort rests on grace already received.

Supply generously. “Supplement” comes from the word for a rich citizen who paid all the costs of a chorus. Not a grudging minimum, but generous investment.

The chain. It starts with faith, the ground. Virtue is moral excellence; knowledge guides it; self-control governs the appetites; steadfastness keeps going under weight; godliness turns all of it towards God; and it ends in brotherly affection and love for all. It moves from God’s gift, through our character, out to other people.

What it does not mean. It is not a ladder to climb one rung at a time, finishing virtue before starting knowledge. The qualities grow together, each feeding the others.

verseByVerse.quote: For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If these qualities are growing in you, your knowledge of Christ will be fruitful. Whoever lacks them is short-sighted to the point of blindness, having forgotten that his past sins were washed away.

Increasing. Peter expects growth to be normal. A static Christian life is already a warning sign.

Ineffective and unfruitful. You can hold accurate doctrine and be entirely unproductive in it.

Short-sighted. He sees what is close, this week’s appetite or grievance, but nothing at a distance: not eternity, not his own story.

The root. He has forgotten that he was cleansed. Not lost the cleansing, but lost the memory of it. Gratitude is the engine of growth.

On a Tuesday. If your spiritual life feels stuck, the answer may not be a new technique. Sit down and remember: what were you, and what has Christ forgiven you? Let thanksgiving restart the engine.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall. For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So be all the more eager to confirm that God has called and chosen you. If you practise these qualities you will never fall, and you will be given a rich welcome into Christ’s eternal kingdom.

What “confirm” means. Not making God’s election secure; that is his act and is settled. It means making it firm in our own assurance. The fruit does not create the root; it shows it. This is how the Reformed tradition reads the verse: not works that secure salvation, but works that confirm it.

Kind counsel. An anxious Christian is not told to search his memory for a decisive moment, or to look inward for a feeling, but to look for growth in ordinary character, which others can see too.

Does perseverance depend on us? The qualities are the fruit of the power that has given us everything (v. 3). Those who belong to Christ are kept by him (John 10:28–29). Our diligence is the way his keeping works out in our lives, not a rival to it.

Never fall. Not a promise of sinlessness, but of not coming to ruin.

A rich entrance. The verb is the same “supply generously” of v. 5. We are to supply these qualities generously; God will generously supply our welcome home. That is cause for praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — Eyewitnesses and the Prophetic Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter knows he will soon die, as Jesus told him, so he keeps reminding them of what they already know. Their faith does not rest on clever myths: the apostles saw Christ’s majesty and heard the Father’s voice on the mountain. And they have the prophetic word, confirmed by that event, a lamp in a dark place until the day dawns. No prophecy came from the prophet’s own understanding; men spoke from God as the Holy Spirit carried them along.
verseByVerse.theology:
Carried Along

Prophecy did not come from the prophet's own interpretation. Men spoke from God as the Holy Spirit carried them along — fully human, and fully God's word.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter wrote knowing his death was near, and arranged for his readers to remember.

Now: Scripture is a lamp in a dark place — enough light until the day dawns.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth that you have. I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder, since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter will keep reminding them of these things, though they already know them, because he knows he will soon die, as Jesus told him, and he wants them to remember after he has gone.

Reminders. Most of what a church needs is not new information, but the same truth said again. Knowing something and having it present to you are different. “Stir you up” means to wake someone.

This tent. His body is temporary accommodation. Jesus had told him how he would die (John 21:18–19). Peter carried that knowledge for thirty years, and his response was to make sure the church would remember the truth. This letter is part of that care.

On a Tuesday. A grandfather writes letters to his grandchildren to be opened after his death, telling them what Christ has meant to him. That is Peter’s instinct: use the time you have to leave the truth behind you.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus had told Peter how he would die.

verseByVerse.quote: For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For when he received honor and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased," we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles did not invent stories about Christ’s power and coming. They saw his majesty and heard the Father’s voice from heaven, “This is my beloved Son”, when they were with him on the holy mountain.

Not myths. The false teachers called Christ’s coming a story. Peter answers with history: we were there.

Eyewitnesses. The word (epoptai) was used in the mystery religions of the highest initiates, those who had “seen”. Peter applies it to a real event on a real mountain.

The voice. He leaves out the shining face and the shelters he wanted to build. He reports the Father’s testimony, because the argument is about testimony.

For worship. The glory the apostles glimpsed is the glory Christ will show at his coming. We will see it too.
verseByVerse.note: The “holy mountain” is the Mount of Transfiguration, where Peter, James and John saw Jesus’ glory.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have the prophetic Scriptures, made even more certain, and you should pay attention to them like a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.

More fully confirmed. Peter does not mean Scripture is better evidence than his own eyes. He means the transfiguration confirmed what the prophets wrote. His readers were not on the mountain, but they have the confirmed word.

A lamp. Not the sun, but enough to see the next steps, and essential in the dark. Scripture is sufficient light until Christ comes.

The morning star. The last light before sunrise, and its herald. Christ calls himself “the bright morning star” (Revelation 22:16). His coming is the dawn.

On a Tuesday. Facing a hard decision or a dark season, you may want a sign. God has given you a lamp. Open it, read it slowly, and walk by the light it gives, until the day dawns.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation. For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above all, understand that no prophecy of Scripture came from the prophet’s own understanding. No prophecy was produced by human will; men spoke from God as the Holy Spirit carried them along.

Origin, not interpretation. Verse 21 explains verse 20. Peter is speaking about where prophecy came from, not about who may read it.

What it does not mean. Roman Catholic teaching has used this verse to argue that only the church can interpret Scripture. But that is not Peter’s point. Every believer is called to read and understand Scripture (Acts 17:11), humbly, in the fellowship of the church and with its teachers, testing all interpretation by Scripture itself.

Carried along. A sailing word, used of Paul’s ship driven by the wind (Acts 27:15). The writers were real men, with their own style; Isaiah does not sound like Amos. Yet the direction was God’s. Scripture is fully human and fully God’s word.

A textual note. The KJV reads “holy men of God spake”. Most early manuscripts read “men spoke from God”, which the ESV follows. The meaning is the same: the source of Scripture is God.

For worship. When you open your Bible, God is speaking. Read with reverence and expectation.

1.theology:
The chapter's great theological claim is 'partakers of the divine nature' (v. 4). This is not deification in the Orthodox sense (we do not become God or merge into the divine essence) nor pantheism (we do not become part of God). It is moral participation: through the Spirit and through union with Christ, God's own character — his holiness, patience, love, truthfulness — is communicated to the believer. Calvin read it as a sharing in God's qualities, not in his essence. The Reformed doctrine of sanctification is nothing less than the outworking of this participation: the divine nature expressing itself in human virtue.

The doctrine of Scripture (vv. 20–21) is equally central. Scripture is not a human document about God; it is God's own word spoken through human instruments. The Spirit carried the prophets; therefore the prophets' words carry divine authority. This is why Peter can call the prophetic word 'more fully confirmed' — the written word outlasts the eyewitness, is available to all, and carries the authority not of human testimony but of the Spirit who inspired it.
1.examples:
The virtue chain (vv. 5–7) addresses a perennial pastoral problem: Christians who park at faith and see no need to move. 'I believe — isn't that enough?' Peter's answer: faith is the beginning, not the destination. A Christian who has been given the divine nature and is not building virtue, knowledge, and love is like a person given a magnificent musical instrument who never practices. The gift is real; the neglect is also real; and the result is the same — no music. Note that Peter does not make the virtues the condition of salvation (they flow from faith, not to it) but the evidence of its reality and the trajectory of its growth.

The lamp-and-morning-star image (v. 19) is a pastoral gift for believers who feel that Scripture reading is dry and unproductive. You do not read the Bible because it is always exciting; you read it because you are in a dark place and it is the only lamp available. The darkness is not a reason to put the lamp down. The lamp is precisely what a dark place requires.

2.title: The Anatomy of a False Teacher
2.text: <sup>1</sup>But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction.<sup>2</sup>And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed.<sup>3</sup>And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.<sup>4</sup>For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment;<sup>5</sup>if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly;<sup>6</sup>if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;<sup>7</sup>and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked<sup>8</sup>(for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard);<sup>9</sup>then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,<sup>10</sup>and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones,<sup>11</sup>whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.<sup>12</sup>But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction,<sup>13</sup>suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you.<sup>14</sup>They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!<sup>15</sup>Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing,<sup>16</sup>but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.<sup>17</sup>These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved.<sup>18</sup>For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error.<sup>19</sup>They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.<sup>20</sup>For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first.<sup>21</sup>For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.<sup>22</sup>What the true proverb says has happened to them: "The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire."
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is Peter’s portrait of the false teacher: his method (slipping in quietly), his doctrine (denying the Master), his motive (greed) and his end (judgment already on its way). Three examples from history, the angels, the flood and Sodom, show that God judges the wicked and rescues the godly. Then Peter describes the teachers themselves: arrogant, driven by appetite, greedy like Balaam, preying on new believers.

The key irony is v. 19: they promise freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption. The test of a teacher is not the sophistication of his words but the shape of his life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Arrival and Judgment of False Teachers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: False prophets troubled Israel, and false teachers will trouble the church. They bring in destructive heresies, deny the Master who bought them, and exploit people for money. But history shows how God acts: he did not spare the angels who sinned, the ancient world, or Sodom, yet he preserved Noah and rescued Lot. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the wicked for judgment.
verseByVerse.theology:
Righteous Lot

False teachers arise from within. God did not spare the angels, the ancient world or Sodom — yet he preserved Noah and rescued Lot. He knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the unrighteous for judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Lot, compromised as he was, was tormented by the evil he saw day after day.

Now: Being grieved by the world’s evil is a mark of the righteous; being comfortable with it is the danger.

verseByVerse.quote: But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction. And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just as false prophets arose in Israel, false teachers will arise in the church. They will quietly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Lord who bought them, and bring swift destruction on themselves. Many will follow their immorality, the gospel will be slandered, and in their greed they will exploit people with lies. But their judgment is coming.

From within. Note “among the people”, “among you”. The danger is inside the church, which is why it is hard to name.

Smuggled in. The verb means to bring in alongside. Nothing is announced. “Heresies” means chosen opinions, a man’s preference set against what was delivered.

“The Master who bought them”. Does this mean Christ died to save these false teachers, so that the atonement is for everyone? Some read it so. Reformed readers usually take “bought” as the language of ownership: these men stood within the church and claimed to belong to the Master, or Peter uses Old Testament language for God purchasing his people as a whole (Deuteronomy 32:6). The more likely reading is the second. Peter’s point is their ingratitude: slaves turning on the owner who paid for them. And v. 22 suggests they were never truly changed.

The damage. The gospel’s reputation suffers. Outsiders judge the way of truth by those who carry its name. And “exploit” is a trading word: the congregation becomes the merchandise.

On a Tuesday. A ministry promises blessing in return for a generous “seed gift”. Peter’s warning is plain: when a teacher treats you as a source of income, he is merchandising you. Give gladly to faithful gospel work, but not to those who sell God’s favour.
verseByVerse.note: Much of this chapter closely parallels the letter of Jude.

verseByVerse.quote: For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment; if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly; if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;
verseByVerse.commentary:
God did not spare the angels who sinned, but holds them in darkness for judgment; he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah and seven others; and he burned Sodom and Gomorrah as an example of what will happen to the ungodly.

Three cases. The highest creatures, the whole world, the most notorious cities. If none was spared, false teachers will not be.

Tartarus. The word for hell here, used only here in the New Testament, was a Greek name for the deepest place of confinement. The angels are held in custody until the final judgment.

Which angels? Some take them as the angels who fell with Satan; others link them with the “sons of God” of Genesis 6:2, as Jude 6 may also do, and Peter mentions them just before the flood. Calvin and many Reformed writers read Genesis 6 as the line of Seth. Either way, the point stands: God judges rebellion.

Noah. Peter adds the theme that governs the passage: God not only judged, he preserved. Only eight people. “Herald of righteousness”: Genesis records no sermon, but years of building the ark in public were a proclamation.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” here is Tartarus, a Greek term for the deepest place of punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked (for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard); then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God rescued righteous Lot, who was deeply distressed by the immoral behaviour around him day after day. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the wicked for punishment on the day of judgment.

Righteous Lot? Genesis does not flatter Lot. He chose to live near Sodom, lingered when told to leave, and his family story is grim. Yet Peter calls him righteous three times. That is not sentiment. It describes his standing before God, not an impressive record.

Tormented. The evidence Peter gives is inward: Lot was tortured in soul, “day after day”, by what he saw and heard.

Comfort for the worn down. If the mark of a righteous man in Sodom is that the place still grieves him, then the believer worn down by the evil around him has evidence of grace, not condemnation. Those who are comfortable with it are the ones in danger.

He knows how. The competence is God’s. We do not have to work out how he will rescue us.

On a Tuesday. A Christian nurse comes home from a ward where colleagues mock everything she holds sacred. She feels weary and grieved. Peter would tell her that her grief is a sign of life, and that the Lord who rescued Lot knows how to keep her.
verseByVerse.note: Genesis does not tell of Lot’s inner distress, though Lot did call the men’s intent wicked (Gen 19:7); Peter draws out the inner side of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–22 — The Portrait, and the Washed Sow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The false teachers scoff at spiritual powers that even angels treat with reverence. They act on instinct like animals, feast at the church’s meals while full of lust and greed, and follow Balaam, who loved money from wrongdoing. They are dry springs and rainless clouds, promising freedom while slaves of corruption. Having known the way of righteousness and turned back, they are worse off than before, like a dog returning to its vomit, or a washed pig to the mud.
verseByVerse.theology:
Washed, Not Changed

The false teachers promise freedom while slaves of corruption. The washed sow returns to the mire because her nature was never changed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Like Balaam, they loved gain and preyed on unsteady new believers.

Now: The question is not whether you have been washed, but whether you have been changed.

verseByVerse.quote: and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones, whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God especially judges those who indulge corrupt desires and despise authority. Bold and arrogant, they slander spiritual beings without fear, whereas even angels, far more powerful, do not bring such accusations before the Lord.

Will not be told. “Bold and willful” means daring and self-pleasing: confidence with no outside check.

“The glorious ones”. Most likely angelic beings. The false teachers speak of the unseen world casually, as men who have never considered it real. Angels, who know these powers, speak with restraint (Jude 9).

A lesson. Reverence about what we do not understand is a mark of maturity. Loose talk about the spiritual world usually shows little thought about it.

verseByVerse.quote: But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction, suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you. They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like animals driven by instinct, these men slander what they do not understand, and they will be destroyed. They revel in broad daylight, stain the church’s meals with their deceit, cannot look at a woman without lust, lure unstable people, and have trained their hearts in greed. They are under God’s curse.

Instinct, not reason. They act on appetite without thought, which is why arguing with them achieves little.

Daytime revelling. Even pagans drank at night; carousing by day showed total loss of restraint (1 Thessalonians 5:7).

Blots and blemishes. They sit at the church’s love feast, the opposite of Christ, the lamb “without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19).

Trained in greed. “Trained” is the athlete’s word. Greed has been practised until it is skilled.

Enticing the unsteady. “Entice” is a fishing word: to bait. Predators choose the weakest. The church must protect its new and unstable members.

verseByVerse.quote: Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing, but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have left the right path and followed Balaam, who loved the money he could make by doing wrong, and was rebuked when a donkey spoke and stopped his madness.

Balaam. A real prophet who put his gift up for sale (Numbers 22–24). He could not curse Israel, but later advised Moab how to lead Israel into sin (Numbers 31:16). Like him, these teachers found that religion pays, and shaped their message to keep it paying.

The donkey. The prophet behaved like an animal, so an animal did the prophet’s job. “Madness” is a strong word: Balaam knew what God had said and went anyway.

Mercy in the road. The donkey and the angel were sent to stop him. Even a man that far gone was given an obstacle.

On a Tuesday. If you find yourself bending the truth to keep a client, a donor or a following, remember Balaam. And if God puts an obstacle in your road, a warning, a friend’s rebuke, it may be his mercy.
verseByVerse.note: Balaam was hired to curse Israel for money, and his donkey spoke to rebuke him.

verseByVerse.quote: These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved. For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error. They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These teachers are dry springs and clouds blown by the wind, and utter darkness awaits them. With loud, empty boasts they lure people who have just escaped from error back into lust, promising freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption. People are slaves to whatever masters them.

Promise without delivery. A spring in a dry land promises life; a dry one is deadly. Clouds that pass without rain disappoint every farmer.

Targeting new converts. They aim at those “barely escaping”, still unsteady after leaving an old life at great cost, and tell them they need not have bothered.

Freedom and slavery. “Whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.” Freedom is not having no master; it is having the right one. The man who throws off God’s rule has changed owners, and taken a worse one.

On a Tuesday. A young believer is told that real freedom means doing whatever he feels like. Ask him what is mastering him: his phone, his appetites, other people’s opinions? Christ’s yoke is the only one that sets us free (John 8:36).

verseByVerse.quote: For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first. For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What the true proverb says has happened to them: "The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If those who escaped the world’s corruption through knowing Christ become entangled again and overcome, they are worse off than before. It would have been better never to have known the way of righteousness than to turn away. They are like the dog that returns to its vomit and the washed pig that goes back to the mud.

Real knowledge, real escape. These men were not outsiders. They had genuinely left certain sins and knew the gospel. Jesus said the same of the house swept clean and reoccupied (Matthew 12:45). Knowledge raises the stakes.

Can a true believer be lost? Arminian Christians read this passage so, pointing to “escaped” and “knowledge of our Lord and Savior”. But Peter’s own proverb explains it. The pig has been washed, really and visibly, but not given a new nature. She goes back to the mud because she is still a pig. They were cleaned, not changed. That fits John’s words about those who left: “they were not of us” (1 John 2:19).

The right use. The point is not to make true believers anxious, but to make everyone honest. Have you been washed, or changed? The evidence is what you keep returning to.

For worship. If you find in yourself a new nature that hates the mud you once loved, thank God. That is his work, and he will finish it (Philippians 1:6).

2.theology: The chapter's controlling theological question is the nature of apostasy. Can a person who has genuinely known Christ fall finally away? The Reformed answer: those truly regenerate will persevere (John 10:28–29; Rom 8:38–39). But the visible church contains those who participate in covenant privileges without possessing covenant life — and it is these who can experience the knowledge described in v. 20 and still return to their former state. The dog and pig proverbs define the boundary: the animal's nature is unchanged. External reformation without regeneration leads to greater corruption. This is not a loophole in the doctrine of perseverance; it is the doctrine's honest context.
2.examples: The Balaam portrait (vv. 15–16) gives the congregation diagnostic tools. The false teacher's test is not doctrinal sophistication but financial transparency: What does this teacher gain from what he teaches? Is the teaching shaped by what people want to hear (and therefore what they will pay to hear)? Balaam was a genuine prophet whose gift was real — but the gift became a commodity. The test of authentic ministry is not whether the gifts are real but whether the teacher loves the Lord more than the wages.

3.title: The Day That Is Coming
3.overview:
The final chapter is the letter's destination. Everything in chapters 1 and 2 has been preparation for this: the false teachers are dangerous not merely because they are immoral but because they have attacked the hope — the promise of Christ's return — and by doing so have severed the ethical nerve of the Christian life. If the Day is not coming, why be holy? If the Lord will not appear, why resist the flesh? The scoffers have grasped this logic and pressed it into service of their own licentiousness.

Peter's response is one of the most carefully constructed arguments in the New Testament. He does not simply reassert the promise; he dismantles the philosophical framework on which the denial rests. The scoffers appeal to uniformitarianism: 'all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation' (v. 4). The world operates by uniform natural processes; there is no basis for expecting a divine interruption. Peter's counter-attack is historical and theological: the world has already been interrupted — twice — by the word of God (creation from water, and the flood), and the same word that brought those interventions has promised a third. Uniformitarianism has already been falsified by the history the scoffers claim to cite.

Then comes the pastoral heart of the chapter — the motive for the apparent delay. God is not slow. He is patient — long-suffering, holding back his power — because he is 'not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance' (v. 9). The delay is not absence. It is mercy. Every day before the Day is a day of grace, an open door of repentance. When the Day comes — sudden, certain, like a thief — it will be final. But it will come into a world still being offered the gospel, and that is the point.

The chapter closes with what may be the most ethically charged question in the epistle: 'What sort of people ought you to be?' (v. 11). Not: When will it happen? The return of Christ is not a date to calculate but a character to cultivate. Holiness, godliness, eagerness for the Day, diligence to be found spotless — this is the life shaped by a hope that is certain. And the letter ends where it began: grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity.

In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder,<sup>2</sup>that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,<sup>3</sup>knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires.<sup>4</sup>They will say, "Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation."<sup>5</sup>For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God,<sup>6</sup>and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished.<sup>7</sup>But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.<sup>8</sup>But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.<sup>9</sup>The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.<sup>10</sup>But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.<sup>11</sup>Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness,<sup>12</sup>waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn!<sup>13</sup>But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.<sup>14</sup>Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace.<sup>15</sup>And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him,<sup>16</sup>as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Scoffers and the Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This second letter, like the first, stirs up their sincere mind by reminder (v.1), that they may remember the prophets and the Lord's commandment through their apostles (v.2), knowing that scoffers will come in the last days following their own desires (v.3), saying, 'Where is the promise of his coming? Everything continues as it has from the beginning' (v.4).

They deliberately overlook that the heavens existed long ago and the earth was formed out of water by God's word (v.5), and that by these the world then existing was deluged and perished (v.6); and that by the same word the present heavens and earth are stored up for fire, kept until the day of judgement (v.7). But do not overlook this: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years and a thousand years as one day (v.8). The Lord is not slow but patient, not wishing any to perish but all to reach repentance (v.9). Yet the day will come like a thief; the heavens will pass away with a roar, the elements dissolve, and the earth and its works be laid bare (v.10).
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Slowness but Patience

The world has not always continued as it was: God's word made it and judged it by the flood. The Lord is not slow but patient, and the day will come like a thief.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Scoffers pointed to the death of the first generation as proof that nothing was coming.

Now: The delay is mercy; the right response is repentance, not argument about the timetable.

verseByVerse.quote: This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder, that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'This is now the second letter that I am writing to you.' Peter identifies himself as the author of 1 Peter and treats both letters as one project with one aim.

'In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder.' The waking verb again from 1:13. Peter's settled view of his ministry is that his readers do not need new material; they need rousing.

'Sincere' is a striking word here. It translates a term often explained as 'judged by sunlight' — what a thing looks like when the light gets behind it. Peter credits them with genuineness even as he warns them.

'That you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles.' Two authorities, set side by side without any suggestion that they differ in weight: the Old Testament prophets, and the apostles carrying the Lord's own commandment.

That is a significant sentence for how the early church understood its own writings. Peter puts apostolic teaching in the same bracket as prophetic Scripture — and he will do it explicitly with Paul's letters in verse 16.

Note also 'your apostles'. Not a distant institution but the men who actually brought them the gospel. And the whole defence against what follows is memory — not a new argument but the recollection of what they were already told.
verseByVerse.note: The earlier letter is most likely 1 Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, "Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing.' The construction is emphatic — mockers mocking — and Peter says their arrival is itself predicted. That is a quietly clever move: the appearance of people denying the promise is evidence that the promise was accurately given.

'Following their own sinful desires.' Peter names the motive before he states the argument, and the order is deliberate. Their doctrine has a cause, and the cause is not intellectual. A man who wants the future to be empty has a reason for wanting it.

Then the taunt itself: 'Where is the promise of his coming?'

'For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation.' The argument has two parts and both would have stung. The first generation has died and nothing has happened — a real pastoral problem in a church burying its founders.

And the second is a philosophy: things go on as they always have. It is the assumption that the world is a closed system running on unbroken regularity, and that what has never been observed to happen therefore does not happen. That is a very modern-sounding argument to find in a first-century letter.

The last days are the whole age from Christ’s first coming to his return (Acts 2:17; Heb 1:2). The scoffers were already present in Peter’s day, and they are with us still.

Peter's answer, when it comes, does not dispute the observation. He disputes the conclusion — and he does it by pointing to two occasions when things did not continue as they were.

verseByVerse.quote: For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God, and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished. But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For they deliberately overlook this fact.' The verb means this escapes them by their own choosing — it is willed forgetfulness. Peter does not accuse them of missing the evidence but of declining to look at it, which is the more serious charge.

And what they overlook is creation itself: 'the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God.' The claim that all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation collapses at the word creation. There was a beginning, and it was not a continuation of anything.

'And that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished.' The second interruption. The same water that the world was formed through later destroyed it — which is exactly a case of things not continuing as they were.

So the argument is complete in two strokes. The scoffers say nothing has ever interrupted the regularity; Peter names two occasions when the world's entire state was changed by the word of God, and both are in the Scriptures the scoffers claim to respect.

'But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire.' The phrase 'the same word' is the hinge of the whole passage. One agency made it, one flooded it, and one holds it now. The present stability is not inertia; it is sustained, and by the same voice that could end it.

Was the flood worldwide? Some Christians hold that it covered the whole inhabited region rather than the whole earth. But Genesis says all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered (Gen 7:19), and Peter sets the flood beside the coming judgment of the whole earth by fire. The more likely reading is that the flood was universal.

'Being kept until the day of judgment.' The custody word again, as of the angels in 2:4. Peter's picture of the present universe is not a machine running down but something held in reserve.

verseByVerse.quote: But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But do not overlook this one fact, beloved.' The same verb he used of the scoffers, now turned round with an endearment attached. They deliberately overlook; do not you overlook this.

'That with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.' The line echoes Psalm 90:4, and it is the answer to the delay — though not the answer usually taken from it.

It is not a formula for calculating prophetic timescales. Peter is not supplying a conversion rate, and reading it as one has produced a great deal of nonsense. Notice that the comparison runs both ways, which would make any arithmetic useless: a day is as a thousand years and a thousand years as a day.

What it says is that God does not stand inside time as we do. To a creature with sixty or eighty years, a delay of two millennia is decisive; to the one who made time it is not a delay at all. The scoffers' argument depends entirely on assuming God experiences duration the way they do.

And both halves are needed. A thousand years as one day means the long wait is nothing to him. One day as a thousand years means no single day is trivial to him either — he is not distracted or inattentive during the interval.

Does this mean that the days of creation were long ages, or that history will last six thousand years? No. Peter is speaking of how God relates to time, to explain the delay of Christ’s coming; the verse is not a conversion table. The days of Genesis 1 must be read from Genesis itself, and their plainest reading is ordinary days (Exod 20:11).

Which removes the sting from the taunt without pretending the wait is short. The fathers did fall asleep, and centuries have passed since Peter wrote. The question is only whether that fact means what the scoffers said it meant, and this verse says it does not.

parallels.desc: a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness.' Peter denies the premise directly, and note the qualifier: as some count. The slowness exists only in the reckoning of the people complaining.

'But is patient toward you.' And here is the positive answer, which is the great sentence of the chapter. The delay is not indifference, not incapacity, and not forgetfulness. It is patience — and it is directed at them.

That reframes the whole complaint. Every day the end has not come is a day granted. The scoffers were treating the interval as evidence against God; Peter says it is evidence of his mercy, and that they are standing inside the very thing they are mocking.

'Not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.' The verse has been fought over for centuries and honesty serves better than a slogan.

Some read 'any' and 'all' as universal — God desires the salvation of every person without exception, and Scripture elsewhere speaks that way (Ezek 33:11; 1 Tim 2:4). Others note that Peter is writing to particular readers and says 'patient toward you', so that the 'all' most naturally means all of you, all his own — and that the delay exists so that none of the elect is missing when the day comes.

The second reading fits the immediate grammar better; the first fits the wider scriptural language about God's disposition toward sinners. What neither reading permits is the conclusion the scoffers wanted — that the delay means nothing is coming.

And on either reading the pastoral use is identical, which is presumably why Peter wrote it. If God is holding the door open, the response of anyone still outside it is not to argue about the mechanism but to walk through.

verseByVerse.quote: But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But the day of the Lord will come like a thief.' The image is the Lord's own (Matt 24:43), and Paul uses it too. What it conveys is not stealth for its own sake but unpredictability — the one thing about a burglary that you cannot prepare for is the timing.

Which answers the scoffers' question exactly. They asked where the promise was; Peter says the promise includes the fact that you will not see it coming.

'Then the heavens will pass away with a roar.' The word is onomatopoeic — a rushing, hissing, crackling noise, used of the whirring of wings and the sound of flames. Peter's universe does not end quietly.

'The heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved.' The word for heavenly bodies is stoicheia, the elements — which may mean the celestial lights, or the basic constituents of the material world. Either way the dissolution is total.

Then the last clause, and it is the most important in the verse: 'and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.'

The best manuscripts read found or laid bare rather than 'burned up', and it changes the picture from mere destruction to disclosure. The fire is not chiefly an incinerator but a searchlight. Everything done on this earth will be found out.

Is the day of the Lord a single event, or a series of events with a thousand-year reign between? Premillennial Christians see a sequence: Christ’s return, a thousand-year reign, then the final judgment and new creation. But Peter speaks of one day: the Lord comes like a thief, the old order passes away, and the new heavens and new earth follow (v. 13). The more likely reading is that Christ’s return, the judgment and the renewal of creation belong together to one final day.

Will the earth then be annihilated, or renewed? Some Christians hold that the old creation will be destroyed and replaced, pointing to pass away and dissolved. But Peter compares it to the flood, which cleansed the world rather than abolishing it (v. 6), and says the earth will be exposed, laid bare to judgment. Paul says creation itself will be set free (Rom 8:21). The more likely reading is that the present creation will be purged by fire and renewed, not abolished.

And that is a far more searching thought than annihilation would be. A universe that simply burns cancels the record; a universe that is laid bare produces it. Peter's point against men who were living as they pleased on the assumption that nothing was coming is not that the world will end but that it will be examined.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — New Heavens, and the Last Command
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness (v.11), waiting for and hastening the day of God, when the heavens will be set on fire and the elements melt (v.12)? But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (v.13).

Therefore be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace (v.14), counting the Lord's patience as salvation — as Paul also wrote according to the wisdom given him (v.15), in all his letters, in which some things are hard to understand and which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures (v.16). Knowing this beforehand, take care not to be carried away by the error of lawless people and lose your stability (v.17); but grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory now and to the day of eternity (v.18).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Answer to Error Is Growth

Since everything will be laid bare, live in holiness and godliness while waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells. The last command is to grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter called Paul a beloved brother and counted his letters among the Scriptures.

Now: A growing believer is far harder to uproot than one merely on guard.

verseByVerse.quote: Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn! But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be?' Peter draws the practical conclusion, and it is worth noticing what he does not draw. Not speculation, not date-setting, not withdrawal. What sort of people ought you to be — the question is about character.

'In lives of holiness and godliness.' Both nouns are plural in Greek — holy behaviours, godlinesses — which suggests the concrete and repeated rather than a general disposition. It is worked out in particular acts.

'Waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God.' The second verb is startling. It can mean to be eager for, but its ordinary sense is to speed something up — and Peter has just said the delay is God's patience, waiting for people to reach repentance. If that is why he waits, then the church's own work of repentance and mission is bound up with the timing. That is a dignity given to ordinary Christian obedience which should stop anyone reading it casually.

'Because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved.' The description is repeated, and it is bleak — until verse 13 turns it round.

'But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth.' There is the point of the whole passage. The fire is not the end of the story and it is not the destruction of the material world as such. What follows is a new earth — physical, real, and renewed, exactly as Isaiah promised (Isa 65:17).

'In which righteousness dwells.' And that single clause is the answer to everything chapter 2 described. Peter has spent a chapter on men who exploited the church and got away with it. The world that is coming is one where righteousness is not visiting but resident — at home, which is the force of the verb.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace. And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace.'

'Found' picks up the word from verse 10, where the earth and its works are laid bare. The same verb, and the connection is deliberate: everything will be found out, so be diligent about what is found in you.

And 'without spot or blemish' is another deliberate reversal. The false teachers were 'blots and blemishes' at the church's own feast (2:13); the readers are to be the opposite, which is the description given to Christ himself as the lamb (1 Pet 1:19).

'And count the patience of our Lord as salvation.' Verse 9 restated as a command. The delay is not to be endured but reckoned — actively counted as mercy. It is the accounting verb, and Peter asks them to enter the interval on the right side of the ledger.

'Just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you.' Peter's warmth here is worth pausing on. These two men had a serious public disagreement at Antioch, where Paul opposed him to his face and later wrote it down (Gal 2:11-14). Peter calls him beloved brother and commends his wisdom. There is no trace of the quarrel.

'There are some things in them that are hard to understand.' A refreshingly honest admission from an apostle about another apostle, and a small comfort to anyone who has struggled through Romans.

'Which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.' Two things follow. Difficulty is not the cause of the twisting — the ignorant and unstable are, and they do it to the plain parts too. And Peter has just called Paul's letters Scripture, while Paul was very likely still alive. That is the New Testament recognising itself.
verseByVerse.note: Peter already counts Paul’s letters among “the Scriptures.”

verseByVerse.quote: You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability. But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care.' The whole letter's purpose in a phrase. Peter has not written to inform them about the future but to prepare them, and forewarning is itself the protection.

'That you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability.' The verb 'carried away' is the same one Paul used of Barnabas being led astray at Antioch (Gal 2:13). And stability is the answer to a word that has run through the letter: the unstable souls the false teachers baited (2:14), and the unstable who twist the Scriptures (3:16). Peter's fear is that the steady will be pulled into that instability.

Then the last command, and after two chapters of warning it is not what one expects: 'But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.'

The defence against error is not chiefly vigilance but growth. Peter does not end by telling them to watch the heretics more closely; he tells them to get on with maturing. A tree that is growing is far harder to uproot than one being braced.

And both nouns matter. Grace — because a man who forgets he was cleansed stops growing (1:9). And knowledge — the letter's key word, reclaimed one last time from the men who were peddling a counterfeit. The answer to false knowledge is not less knowledge but the real thing, and it is knowledge of a person.

'To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.' A doxology addressed to Christ, which is itself a statement about who he is. And the phrase 'the day of eternity' occurs nowhere else — Peter, having written a chapter about the day of the Lord and the day of judgement, ends by naming a day that does not end.

These are the last recorded words of the man who denied his Lord in a courtyard, written by someone who knew his death was near. He signs off with glory to the one he had once said he did not know.

3.theology:
Uniformitarianism and the Word of God: Peter's refutation of the scoffers in vv. 5–7 is a model of theological apologetics. The uniformitarians claim that the world operates by consistent natural processes. Peter grants the observation and then shows that the historical record — the record the uniformitarians themselves appeal to — contains two catastrophic interruptions of the very uniformity they invoke: creation and the flood. Both were brought about by the word of God. The same word that did those things has spoken again, and the third act — the fire — is as certain as the first two. The apologist who begins with Scripture's own historical witness is standing on solid ground.

Divine patience and the will of God in salvation: Verse 9 is one of the great texts on the scope of God's salvific will: 'not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.' Reformed theology reads this in its literary context: 'toward you' — the elect community. The 'all' is the full complement of those for whom God's patience is being exercised — all who will come to repentance within the span of his patience. This is not universalism (the Day will still come and shut the door), and it is not a contradiction of election (God's patience is itself the means by which the elect are gathered). It is the breathtaking truth that the apparent delay of the parousia is not divine procrastination — it is divine love, actively gathering those who are his.

New creation as promise: The new heavens and new earth of verse 13 is the eschatological horizon of the entire epistle — and of the entire New Testament. Herman Bavinck's axiom — grace restores nature — finds its ultimate expression here: the fire does not destroy the creation but purifies it; the new creation is this creation glorified, the world God made very good and will make even better. Anthony Hoekema's The Bible and the Future demonstrates that the new earth is not a replacement but a renewal — which is why Christian hope is not escapism but engagement: the world we tend and serve and love matters eternally, because it is the world God intends to redeem.
3.examples:
Then: The scoffers' question — 'Where is the promise of his coming?' — has been asked in every generation. The first generation of believers died; the second, the third, the hundredth. Each generation has faced the apparent delay, and the temptation to conclude that the promise was empty. Peter's answer remains the same across every generation: God is not slow. He is patient. His patience is not weakness — it is mercy in motion, gathering those who are still to be gathered before the door closes. Every generation of Christians lives in the overlap of promise and fulfilment, patience and urgency.

Now: 'What sort of people ought you to be?' (v. 11) is the most searching pastoral question the letter asks, and it lands as heavily today as it did in the first century. The return of Christ has not yet come — but it is coming, and it is certain. The question is not about calculation but about formation. The person who genuinely believes the Day is coming will live differently: with moral seriousness, with urgency about the gospel, with detachment from the world's false securities, with eager longing for righteousness. The Christian who has domesticated eschatology into a theological opinion without ethical bite has not yet let 2 Peter 3 do its work. Let it. Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. That is the whole assignment — and it will last exactly until the Day of eternity.
